claims.text: The initial NbMoTaW alloy is equiatomic and single-phase BCC.
Untreated NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical strength at approximately 1600 °C.
Untreated NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has only been inferred computationally and has not been experimentally validated.
A two-step heat treatment will produce fine, discontinuous B2 precipitates within a continuous disordered BCC matrix in equiatomic NbMoTaW.
The first homogenization step will produce a uniform composition.
Controlled cooling or annealing after homogenization will precipitate fine, dispersed B2 particles in the BCC matrix.
An inverted microstructure consisting of discrete B2 precipitates in a continuous BCC matrix can improve room-temperature ductility while maintaining high strength.
Discontinuous B2 precipitates will pin dislocations and thereby maintain elevated-temperature strength.
Discontinuous B2 precipitates will act as irradiation-defect sinks.
The proposed defect-sink action will reduce voids, amorphization, helium bubbles, and related irradiation damage.
A continuous disordered BCC matrix will enhance room-temperature plasticity by facilitating dislocation motion.
Heat-treated NbMoTaW will have a higher room-temperature fracture strain than untreated NbMoTaW.
Heat-treated NbMoTaW will retain a high-temperature yield strength of approximately 1 GPa or greater at temperatures up to about 1600 °C.
The heat-treated alloy will preserve BCC structural stability up to approximately 1600 °C.
Heat-treated NbMoTaW will exhibit fewer helium bubbles and dislocation loops after helium-ion and heavy-ion irradiation than untreated NbMoTaW.
The predicted irradiation benefit applies under dual-beam helium-ion and heavy-ion exposure at reactor-relevant fluences and energies.
Failure to obtain statistically significant gains in room-temperature ductility and irradiation resistance, or loss of high-temperature strength or BCC stability, would falsify the hypothesis.
